surveyDefinition.title: Smartwatches — consumer survey (Global)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 5 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on usage intensity, purchase drivers, feature priorities, and upgrade/replacement behaviour.

segments.name: Health-Monitoring Owners
segments.description: Own a smartwatch primarily to track health metrics like heart rate, sleep, and blood oxygen; they wear it continuously, including overnight, and prioritise accuracy and data integration with health apps.

segments.name: Performance-Focused Athletes
segments.description: Use the smartwatch as a training tool for running, cycling, or other sports; they demand GPS accuracy, advanced workout modes, and durable hardware, and they upgrade when training features advance.

segments.name: Convenience-Driven Owners
segments.description: Value the smartwatch for notifications, quick replies, and contactless payments; they wear it during the day but often take it off at night, and they prioritise ease of use and battery life over advanced sensors.

segments.name: Style-Led Owners
segments.description: Choose a smartwatch that looks like a traditional watch or complements their personal style; they are willing to trade some functionality for aesthetics and prefer customisable bands and premium materials.

segments.name: Budget-Conscious Buyers
segments.description: Seek the lowest price that covers basic smartwatch functions; they are highly price-sensitive, compare deals, and may delay upgrades or choose older models to stay within budget.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Smartwatches buyers worldwide. It asks how people use Smartwatches, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories. This global view is not a separate fieldwork exercise: it selects the strongest questions from the regional surveys and blends their percentages using population-style regional weights.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults worldwide who buy or use Smartwatches for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Adults who currently own or intend to purchase a smartwatch within the next 12 months; Must be the primary decision-maker and payer for the device; Must use the smartwatch for personal, non-work purposes (or mixed use is acceptable). Excluded: Children under 18 (unless parent proxy is needed for kids' smartwatches); Businesses or institutions purchasing smartwatches in bulk for employees; People who only use basic fitness bands without smart features.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Consumers buy smartwatches for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide on the model and brand themselves. While some businesses may purchase smartwatches for employees, the dominant market is individual consumers purchasing for themselves.
respondentBehaviours: Uses smartphone (iOS or Android) as primary device
Values fitness tracking, health monitoring, notifications, and convenience
Researches online reviews and compares brands before purchase
Upgrades every 2-4 years or when new features launch
Engages with apps and ecosystems (Apple Health, Google Fit, etc.)
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are simulated from a persona-weighted panel of 2,500 synthetic respondents built from real market evidence, not from fieldwork. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

sections.label: Smartwatch Usage & Lifestyle Context
sections.covers: Establishes how respondents use their smartwatch in daily life, including wear occasions, frequency, and the primary jobs it is hired to do.

sections.label: Purchase Journey & Decision Drivers
sections.covers: Covers the triggers, research process, channel choice, and the factors that ultimately decide which smartwatch is bought.

sections.label: Feature Priorities & Trade-offs
sections.covers: Explores which smartwatch features are must-haves, how quality is judged, and what buyers are willing to give up when forced to choose.

sections.label: Satisfaction, Retention & Upgrade Outlook
sections.covers: Measures satisfaction with the current device, identifies pain points and switching triggers, and gauges future upgrade intentions.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing who owns or intends to buy a smartwatch and how they wear it in daily life, revealing the primary jobs the device is hired for. It then traces the purchase journey from trigger to channel and spend, and the decision drivers that separate brand-loyal upgraders from price-driven switchers. Next, it drills into feature priorities and trade-offs, forcing respondents to reveal what they truly value and what they would sacrifice. Finally, it measures satisfaction, pain points, and future upgrade intent, closing the loop on retention and churn risk. The arc moves…

metadata.segmentation_lens: Jobs-to-be-done combined with usage intensity: the same smartwatch is hired for fundamentally different jobs (health monitoring, fitness training, notification convenience, style, or outdoor durability), and the depth of engagement with those jobs separates buyers more meaningfully than simple frequ

segments.name: Health-Monitoring Owners
segments.description: Own a smartwatch primarily to track health metrics like heart rate, sleep, and blood oxygen; they wear it continuously, including overnight, and prioritise accuracy and data integration with health apps.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report the highest frequency of continuous wear, the strongest demand for health-sensor accuracy, and the greatest willingness to pay for advanced health features.

segments.name: Performance-Focused Athletes
segments.description: Use the smartwatch as a training tool for running, cycling, or other sports; they demand GPS accuracy, advanced workout modes, and durable hardware, and they upgrade when training features advance.
segments.hypothesis: This group will show the highest engagement with workout-specific features, the highest tolerance for higher price points, and the lowest interest in style or notification features.

segments.name: Convenience-Driven Owners
segments.description: Value the smartwatch for notifications, quick replies, and contactless payments; they wear it during the day but often take it off at night, and they prioritise ease of use and battery life over advanced sensors.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report moderate usage frequency, high importance of notification and payment features, and lower willingness to pay for health-specific capabilities.

segments.name: Style-Led Owners
segments.description: Choose a smartwatch that looks like a traditional watch or complements their personal style; they are willing to trade some functionality for aesthetics and prefer customisable bands and premium materials.
segments.hypothesis: This group will rate design and brand reputation as top decision drivers, show lower interest in advanced health metrics, and be less likely to upgrade frequently unless a new style is released.

segments.name: Budget-Conscious Buyers
segments.description: Seek the lowest price that covers basic smartwatch functions; they are highly price-sensitive, compare deals, and may delay upgrades or choose older models to stay within budget.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report the lowest spend bands, the highest sensitivity to price in trade-offs, and the longest upgrade cycles, often waiting for sales or promotions.

segmentModel.tie_break: Question cp5 (Which of these jobs does your smartwatch do for you on a regular basis?) is the most direct behavioural self-report because it asks respondents to identify the primary functions they actually use, which maps almost one-to-one to the segment definitions (health tracking, workout guidance, notifications, style).
notes: Segments are reachable: each has at least two scoring options and at least one 3-point option.
Some options are intentionally left unscored because they do not discriminate (e.g., cp1, cp7, cp8, bb3, bb4, sf1, sf7).
Budget-conscious segment is primarily identified by price sensitivity and upgrade delay, with some supporting signals from purchase behaviour.
21 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=250 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are simulated from a persona-weighted panel, not fielded with real respondents. Replace with primary data after fielding.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.
